question: Caller ID shows your bank's real name and phone number. What does that prove?

options.text: The call is definitely genuine
Nothing — caller ID can be spoofed just as easily as an email display name
It proves the caller has been verified by the bank
It means the call is encrypted

explanation: A phone showing a bank's real name and number proves nothing about who's actually calling — spoofing caller ID is straightforward and common.

question: A caller claiming to be from your bank's fraud team asks you to read back a one-time code you just received by text. What should you do?

options.text: Read it back — they're trying to help protect your account
Refuse — a real bank never asks you to read back a one-time code, since that code exists to prove a request came from you, not them
Read it back only if they sound professional
Ask them to text you a different code first

explanation: That code is a genuine one-time password — sharing it hands over exactly what it was designed to protect against. The text itself typically says not to share it, which the caller is asking you to override.

question: Why are AI-cloned voices making vishing more dangerous?

options.text: They aren't actually a meaningful threat yet
They can imitate a real bank's tone or even a specific person's voice, defeating "I'd recognize that voice" as a safety check
They only work over landlines
They require the victim's cooperation to even function

explanation: Voice cloning and caller ID spoofing together are cited as one of the fastest-growing threats to individuals and small businesses, since they defeat both major ways people used to sanity-check a call.

question: A caller says your account will be compromised unless you act in the next few minutes. What does that pressure usually indicate?

options.text: A genuine emergency requiring immediate action
An attempt to stop you from pausing to verify the call independently
Standard bank fraud-prevention procedure
A technical requirement of the phone system

explanation: If a call creates pressure to act immediately, that pressure is itself a red flag, regardless of how calm or official the caller sounds.

question: What's the safest way to handle a suspicious call claiming to be your bank?

options.text: Continue the call and provide the information requested
Hang up and call back using the number on your card or statement, not one the caller gives you
Ask the caller for their employee ID number
Stay on the line but simply refuse to answer questions

explanation: Calling back on a number you already trust sidesteps the entire call — there's no need to judge whether the caller is legitimate if you verify independently instead.
